teachingPoints.objective: Preserve the pilot's accented tree target.

Recall both default stress mappings with cluster/y limits.
teachingPoints.prompt: Recall the n/s/vowel stress shortcut, its syllable mapping, and the qualifications for consonant clusters and final y.
teachingPoints.answer: n, s, vowel → llana default; other consonants → aguda default. Llana means second-to-last stress; aguda means final stress. The n/s shortcut applies only when n or s is not preceded by another consonant; final y counts as a consonant.
teachingPoints.explanation: Robots follows the other-consonant default; bíceps needs a tilde for llana stress. This cue summarizes general stress, not hiatus or diacritic exceptions.

teachingPoints.objective: Apply the full qualified llana accent condition.
teachingPoints.prompt: When does a llana, stressed on the second-to-last syllable, need a tilde under the general rules?

teachingPoints.prompt: When does an aguda, stressed on the last syllable, need a written tilde?

teachingPoints.prompt: What does the lean-on mnemonic mean for diacritic pairs, and why is it not a universal accent rule?
teachingPoints.answer: It associates the stressed member with pronouns like tú, question words like qué and affirmation sí; stressed té and sé still require their learned meanings. Emphasis alone does not license a tilde.

teachingPoints.objective: Recall exact WEIRDO expansion, trigger mapping and limits.
teachingPoints.prompt: Expand WEIRDO, map each letter to a trigger category and example, and state what the mnemonic does not guarantee.
teachingPoints.answer: WEIRDO means an odd person. W = Wishes/volition (querer que); E = Emotions (alegrarse de que); I = Impersonal expressions (es posible que); R = Recommendations (recomendar que); D = Doubt/denial (dudar que); O = Ojalá (I hope/if only). It is a memory cue, not an exhaustive or exception-free rule.

teachingPoints.objective: Preserve feminine gender despite exceptional un/algún/ningún.
teachingPoints.prompt: Why can un águila, algún águila and ningún águila occur even though águila is feminine?
teachingPoints.answer: Uno, alguno and ninguno also shorten before feminine nouns beginning with stressed a or ha; the noun remains feminine.

teachingPoints.objective: Shorten ninguno before masculine problema.

teachingPoints.objective: Restore the full adjective after the noun.
teachingPoints.prompt: Es un amigo ___. (good; put the adjective after the noun)

teachingPoints.sourceSection: What Apocopates Before a Masculine Singular Noun
teachingPoints.objective: Apply masculine singular ordinal shortening.
teachingPoints.prompt: Vivo en el ___ piso. (third)

teachingPoints.objective: Retain apocope despite an intervening modifier.
teachingPoints.prompt: Fue el ___ y único intento. (primero)

teachingPoints.objective: Praise importance rather than physical size.
teachingPoints.prompt: Cervantes fue un ___ escritor. (Cervantes was a great writer)

teachingPoints.objective: Explain the common size/quality position contrast.
teachingPoints.prompt: How does una gran ciudad usually differ from una ciudad grande?
teachingPoints.answer: The first praises a great city; the second describes a physically big city.

teachingPoints.objective: Keep grande after comparative más.
teachingPoints.prompt: Es la más ___ ciudad de la región. (big)

teachingPoints.sourceSection: Santo → San (Before Most Male Saints' Names)
teachingPoints.objective: Retain the full saint/holy word.

teachingPoints.sourceSection: Santo → San (Before Most Male Saints' Names)
teachingPoints.objective: Use the normal male saint-name shortening.
teachingPoints.prompt: ___ Pedro. (Saint Peter)

teachingPoints.sourceSection: Santo → San (Before Most Male Saints' Names)
teachingPoints.objective: Qualify the Do-/To- memory aid.
teachingPoints.prompt: Which Santo exceptions does the Do-/To- memory cue recall, and what is its limit?
teachingPoints.answer: Santo Domingo, Santo Tomás, Santo Tomé and Santo Toribio; the cue recalls these names rather than predicting every Do-/To- name.
teachingPoints.explanation: Do maps to Domingo; To maps to Tomás, Tomé and Toribio. Female saint names retain Santa.

teachingPoints.objective: Use cien for exactly one hundred.
teachingPoints.prompt: Hay ___ personas. (100)

teachingPoints.objective: Retain ciento inside a compound number.
teachingPoints.prompt: Hay ___ veinte libros. (120)

teachingPoints.objective: Understand the unrestricted-choice indefinite.
Shorten cualquiera even with a feminine noun.
teachingPoints.prompt: ___ mujer puede participar. (Any woman)

teachingPoints.objective: Separate literary plural from selecting one member.
teachingPoints.prompt: What register does cualesquiera have, and how would you commonly say any one of the books?
teachingPoints.answer: It is rare or literary; cualquiera de los libros selects any one of the books.

exclusions.reason: Recombines already represented saint names, ordinals, buen, gran and ningún.

teachingPoints.objective: Retain the recent-completion periphrasis.
teachingPoints.meaning: to have just done (with an infinitive; present or imperfect in these examples)

teachingPoints.objective: Conjugate the auxiliary, not the action.
teachingPoints.prompt: Which verb is conjugated in the Spanish construction for having just done something?
teachingPoints.answer: Acabar is conjugated, followed by de and an infinitive.

teachingPoints.objective: Preserve Spain's informal plural and accent.
teachingPoints.prompt: Vosotros ___ de llegar. (You have just arrived; Spain, informal plural)

teachingPoints.objective: Distinguish recency from literal completion.
teachingPoints.prompt: How does Acabé de comer differ from Acabo de comer?
teachingPoints.answer: Acabé de comer means I finished eating; Acabo de comer means I have just eaten.

teachingPoints.objective: Anchor a brother's just-completed call now.
teachingPoints.prompt: Mi hermano ___ de llamar. (My brother just called)

teachingPoints.objective: Anchor recent arrival before the past call.
teachingPoints.prompt: ___ de llegar cuando sonó el teléfono. (I had just arrived.)

teachingPoints.objective: Retain the verb's literal meaning.
Place the masculine object before acabo.
teachingPoints.prompt: ___ acabo de comprar. (I just bought it [el libro])

teachingPoints.objective: Move the object to the infinitive.
teachingPoints.prompt: Rewrite Te acabo de llamar with the object attached to the infinitive.

exclusions.reason: Repeated present/imperfect recent-past applications, with no separate rule or mnemonic.

teachingPoints.objective: Connect literal carrying to duration usage.
teachingPoints.meaning: to carry; with duration and a gerund, to have been doing

teachingPoints.objective: Recall the carrying-time image and mapping.
teachingPoints.prompt: What does the carrying-time image help remember about llevar with a gerund?
teachingPoints.answer: Llevar literally means to carry; figuratively it carries accumulated time spent doing an action that continues.
teachingPoints.explanation: Map llevar to the conjugated verb, the time carried to the duration, and the activity to the gerund.

teachingPoints.objective: Avoid an invented ban on perfect progressives.
teachingPoints.prompt: Does learning Llevo cinco años viviendo aquí make He estado viviendo aquí cinco años ungrammatical?
teachingPoints.answer: No. The perfect progressive can be grammatical; llevar clearly emphasizes accumulated ongoing duration.

teachingPoints.objective: Allow duration on either side of gerund.
teachingPoints.prompt: Must the duration come before leyendo in a llevar duration construction?
teachingPoints.answer: No. Llevo dos horas leyendo and Llevo leyendo dos horas are both possible.

teachingPoints.objective: Express accumulated study duration continuing now.
teachingPoints.prompt: ___ tres horas estudiando. (I've been studying for three hours)

teachingPoints.objective: Use infinitive, not gerund, after sin.
teachingPoints.prompt: Llevo una semana sin ___. (smoking)

teachingPoints.sourceSection: Imperfect: "Had Been Doing X For Y"
teachingPoints.objective: Measure ongoing duration at a past moment.
teachingPoints.prompt: ___ dos años viviendo en Madrid cuando lo conocí. (I had been living there.)

teachingPoints.sourceSection: Question Form: "How Long Have You Been…?"
teachingPoints.objective: Ask for duration with cuánto tiempo.
teachingPoints.prompt: ¿___ tiempo llevas estudiando español? (How long?)

teachingPoints.sourceSection: Question Form: "How Long Have You Been…?"
teachingPoints.objective: Retain the Spain informal plural question form.
teachingPoints.prompt: ¿Cuántos años ___ viviendo aquí? (vosotros; Spain, informal plural)

teachingPoints.objective: Measure time without speaking to someone.
teachingPoints.prompt: ___ dos semanas sin hablar con él. (I haven't spoken to him in 2 weeks)

exclusions.reason: Recombines ongoing and negative duration already represented.
Restates the four duration patterns; its carrying-time aid is separately inventoried near the core.

teachingPoints.objective: Use present for study continuing now.
teachingPoints.prompt: Hace dos años que ___ español. (estudiar; I still study it.)

teachingPoints.sourceSection: Construction 2: Present + Desde Hace + Time (Same Meaning)
teachingPoints.objective: Retain the elapsed-duration connective.
teachingPoints.meaning: for (an elapsed duration continuing to the reference point)

teachingPoints.sourceSection: Construction 2: Present + Desde Hace + Time (Same Meaning)
teachingPoints.objective: Transform time-first into activity-first duration.
teachingPoints.prompt: Rewrite Hace dos años que estudio español starting with Estudio español.
teachingPoints.answer: Estudio español desde hace dos años.

teachingPoints.objective: Place a completed arrival an hour ago.
teachingPoints.prompt: Hace una hora ___. (llegar; I arrived an hour ago.)

teachingPoints.objective: Do not infer ongoing duration from que alone.
teachingPoints.prompt: Can hace… que occur with a preterite event meaning time ago?
teachingPoints.answer: Yes. Que may appear there too; inspect the verb tense and context, not just que.

teachingPoints.objective: Supply impersonal hace for continuing residence.
teachingPoints.prompt: ___ dos años que vivo en Madrid. (I've been living in Madrid for 2 years)

teachingPoints.objective: Contrast continuing duration with completed past study.
teachingPoints.prompt: How do Hace dos años que estudio and Hace dos años estudié differ?
teachingPoints.answer: The first means I have been studying for two years and still do; the second places completed studying two years ago.

teachingPoints.objective: Interpret past-arrival questions as time ago.
teachingPoints.prompt: Does ¿Cuánto tiempo hace que llegaste? ask about an ongoing arrival?
teachingPoints.answer: No. It asks how long ago you arrived; llegaste is preterite.

teachingPoints.objective: Negate the activity after que.
teachingPoints.prompt: Hace dos meses que ___ lo veo. (I have not seen him.)

teachingPoints.objective: Connect elapsed time to present acquaintance.
teachingPoints.prompt: Hace dos años ___ a Andrés. (I've known Andrés for 2 years)

exclusions.reason: Repeated applications of the three constructions and their negative, all explicitly inventoried.

teachingPoints.objective: Retain the habitual auxiliary's meaning.
teachingPoints.meaning: to usually do; to tend to (followed by an infinitive)

teachingPoints.objective: Conjugate soler while retaining infinitive breakfast.
teachingPoints.prompt: Yo ___ desayunar a las ocho. (I usually have breakfast.)

teachingPoints.objective: Keep o in unstressed nosotros.
teachingPoints.prompt: Nosotros ___ cenar tarde. (soler)

teachingPoints.objective: Retain Spain's soléis with its accent.
teachingPoints.prompt: Vosotros ___ cenar tarde. (soler; Spain, informal plural)

teachingPoints.objective: Distinguish restricted usage from nonexistent forms.
teachingPoints.prompt: Does soler's restricted usage mean suela and ha solido are impossible?
teachingPoints.answer: No. Those forms exist; present and imperfect indicative are the main everyday habit forms taught here.

teachingPoints.objective: Describe childhood habits with solía.
teachingPoints.prompt: De niño, ___ jugar en el parque. (As a kid, I used to play in the park)

teachingPoints.objective: Explain explicit regularity versus neutral present.
teachingPoints.prompt: What does Suelo estudiar add to neutral Estudio?
teachingPoints.answer: It explicitly marks studying as what I usually do, a recurring habit.

teachingPoints.objective: Express not usually without asserting never.
teachingPoints.prompt: ___ ___ ver la televisión por la mañana. (I don't usually watch TV in the morning)

exclusions.reason: Reuses present, imperfect and negative habits without a new teaching point.
